```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(ecoeval)
ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "ecoeval")
```

Before any accuracy number can be computed, ecoeval has to decide which AI row
corresponds to which gold row. A person looking at two rows side by side can
often tell they describe the same interaction even when the text doesn't match,
where an automated matcher can't. That's why the app lets you review and correct
the pairings.

## Which papers are compared

ecoeval compares the papers both sides have, and within those papers every
record from both sides. Each side's papers come from its paper list when one is
supplied, and otherwise from the papers its records mention. Within the compared
papers, some records pair up and some don't.

```{r}
schema <- read_schema(ex("schema.json"))
ai   <- prepare_records(read_table_any(ex("ai_records.csv")),   "doi", prefix = "a")
gold <- prepare_records(read_table_any(ex("gold_records.csv")), "doi", prefix = "g")

ai_papers   <- prepare_papers(read_table_any(ex("ai_papers.csv")),   "doi")
gold_papers <- prepare_papers(read_table_any(ex("gold_papers.csv")), "doi")

scope <- compute_scope(paper_set(ai, ai_papers), paper_set(gold, gold_papers))
lengths(scope)
```

Papers only one side has are left out and don't count against either side. A
paper only the gold standard has just isn't compared, and gets no warning.

Paper links decide which papers are compared; they don't affect the scores
directly. The two kinds of mistake have different costs. A *missed* paper link
only leaves that paper out. A *wrong* paper link compares one paper's records
against another's, so every number for it is meaningless. The paper-link review
is there to catch wrong links.

## How two values are compared

Each pair of values goes through a series of steps, **exact → normalized →
fuzzy → AI reviewer**, and each step only sees the values the step before it
couldn't match. So the slower, more expensive steps only run on a small share of
cells.

```{r}
compare_pair("predation", "predation", "fuzzy")$rung
compare_pair("Predation ", "predation", "fuzzy")$rung
compare_pair("Myotis lucifugus", "Myotis lucifigus", "fuzzy")$rung
```

A field's comparison setting is the **last** step it may reach, so a field set
to exact matching never accepts a fuzzy match:

```{r}
compare_pair("Predation", "predation", "exact")$agree
compare_pair("Myotis lucifugus", "Myotis lucifigus", "normalized")$agree
```

The defaults come from each field's type in the JSON Schema:

```{r}
schema$fields[, c("field", "type", "comparator")]
```

Without normalisation, the first run shows a lot of disagreements that are
really just formatting. Two of the defaults handle that:

```{r}
compare_pair("10", "10.0", "numeric")$agree
compare_pair("2021-03-08", "08/03/2021", "date")$agree
```

Dates need care. `strptime()` ignores trailing characters, so a simple parser
reads `"05/01/2020"` under `"%Y/%m/%d"` as the year 5. `parse_date_loose()` only
accepts a format when the parsed date converts back to the original text.

## Two ways of using an LLM, for different columns

|                            | How it works                           | Cached per   | Best for                    |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------ | --------------------------- |
| **Normalize, then compare** | convert both values to a standard form | **value**    | species names               |
| **AI reviewer**            | read the pair, return a verdict and why | **pair**    | supporting sentences, prose |

The AI reviewer runs after matching, never before it. Matching considers every
possible pair within a paper: 5 AI records against 5 gold records is 25 pairs,
times the number of linkage fields, in LLM calls. Normalisation works per value:
10 values take 10 calls, and the comparisons after that are cheap. So
normalisation grows with the number of values, and running the reviewer during
matching would grow with the square of it.

So the order is:

1. Pick linkage fields and comparisons
2. **Normalise the linkage fields** on both sides, per value and cached. This
   does nothing if no field uses a normalising comparison
3. Run the matcher on the normalised values
4. Score the cells with the plain comparisons. The AI reviewer then runs per
   paper, on paired records only, for the cells the plain comparisons couldn't
   settle

Two things follow from that order. The app **shows the original values and
compares the normalised ones**. And **the granularity check uses normalised
values**, so `"M. lucifugus"` and `"Myotis lucifugus"` count as the same.

With no API key set up, cells that need the AI reviewer are marked as *pending*
instead of getting a verdict:

```{r}
res <- compare_pair("bats ate moths", "moths were taken by bats", "judge")
c(agree = res$agree, rung = res$rung, pending = res$pending)
```

Verdicts are cached per pair and saved in `run_config.json`. An LLM can answer
differently each time it's asked, so saving the verdicts keeps a run
reproducible.

## The matcher

The matcher works one paper at a time, pairs each record with at most one
record on the other side, and **only links two records when it judges that more
likely than not**. Gold standards hold records the extraction missed, and
extractions hold records the gold standard doesn't have. If a leftover gold
record were paired with whatever AI record was free in the same paper, a missed
record would show up as a disagreement. So two records are only linked when
their identity columns support it. You can link records the matcher left apart,
and reject links it got wrong.

Each identity column of a candidate pair is scored *agree*, *close*, or
*differ* by string similarity, and a Fellegi-Sunter model weighs each result
for or against the two rows being the same record. Agreeing on a species name
is strong evidence, because two different records rarely share one by chance.
Agreeing on an interaction type with four possible values is weak evidence,
because different records often do.

A single paper has too few records to learn those weights from, so the model is
fitted **once across all compared records** and then applied paper by paper. How
often two different records agree by chance is learned from pairs in
*different* papers, which can't be the same record. How often a record agrees
with itself is learned from pairs within a paper, kept close to a starting
estimate so that a small dataset can't push the model to extreme values.

```{r}
config  <- default_comparator_config(schema)
linkage <- config$field[config$linkage]
linkage

paper_map <- tibble::tibble(ai_paper = scope$papers, gold_paper = scope$papers)
fit_linkage_model(ai, gold, linkage, paper_map)

pairs <- align_records(ai, gold, linkage, paper_map)
table(pairs$kind)
```

`min_posterior` on `align_records()` sets how sure the matcher must be to link
two records. The default is 0.5.

**Each record is paired at most once.** Records left over on either side count
as false positives and false negatives. An extra AI record counts as a false
positive whether it came from a hallucination or a deduplication failure. To
tell which, look at the granularity warning.

## The three manual corrections

For **rows**, you can fix the pairing: reject a link, or link two unpaired
records. For **cells**, you can fix the verdict: say that two values mean the
same thing, or that they don't.

Linking two unpaired records is the correction you'll need most. The matcher
tends to miss pairs whose identifying values are written differently, and a
person can usually recognise those as the same record. Rejecting a link can
only remove pairs, so without manual linking you couldn't add the pairs the
matcher missed.

All three update every metric straight away and are saved in
`run_config.json`. The app also shows how many corrections were made by hand:

```{r}
correction_count(
  rejected  = data.frame(ai_rid = character(0), gold_rid = character(0)),
  added     = data.frame(ai_rid = "a1", gold_rid = "g1"),
  overrides = data.frame(pair_id = c("p1", "p2"), field = "x", agree = TRUE)
)
```

## When to review by hand

You don't have to check every row. After a full scoring run, ecoeval can list
the pairs that look wrong, so you can review a few papers instead of all of
them:

```{r}
cells <- score_cells(pairs, ai, gold, config)
suspect_pairs(cells, linkage)
```

A pair is listed in two cases. If it agrees on **nothing**, it's almost
certainly two unrelated records the matcher joined. If it disagrees on every
**identity column**, it may still agree on other columns like country and year,
but the columns that say which record it is all disagree.

## Granularity: do the two datasets split records the same way?

ecoeval groups the gold records in each paper by the chosen linkage fields and
counts groups with more than one record. If many records share the same
values, the person who made the gold standard split records by something the
linkage fields don't include.

```{r}
granularity_check(gold, linkage, "gold")
```

The two gold records in that paper differ only by year, and year isn't a
linkage field. Add a linkage field and try again, or treat it as a finding: the
two datasets split records differently.

## When the extraction is more detailed than the gold standard

Sometimes the extraction splits one gold record into several rows, for example
twelve rows by size class where the gold standard has one row with the total
count. Matched one to one, one of the twelve pairs with the gold record and the
other eleven count as false positives.

Rolling up the extraction fixes this. Its records are grouped within each paper
by the fields you choose, numeric fields such as a quantity are added up, and
the grouped rows are matched against the gold standard. The gold standard is
never rolled up. The grouping rules are the same as ecoreview's.

```{r}
ai_rows <- tibble::tibble(
  .rid = sprintf("a%05d", 1:4), .paper = "P1",
  species = c("Pterois volitans", "Pterois volitans", "Pterois volitans",
              "Amphiprion ocellaris"),
  size_class = c("small", "medium", "large", NA),
  quantity = c(10, 20, 30, 5)
)
gold_rows <- tibble::tibble(
  .rid = c("g00001", "g00002"), .paper = "P1",
  species = c("Pterois volitans", "Amphiprion ocellaris"),
  quantity = c(60, 5)
)
rollup_extraction(ai_rows, by = "species", sum = "quantity")
```

`suggest_rollup()` tries grouping by each combination of the identity columns
and picks the one that pairs the most gold records, preferring groupings whose
totals match the gold standard's numbers:

```{r}
s <- suggest_rollup(ai_rows, gold_rows, "species", "quantity")
s$by
s$sum
s$summary
```

In the app, the suggestion appears on the field-mapping screen and above the
comparison grid, and a tick box switches the roll-up on and off. Pass
`rollup_by` and `rollup_sum` to `run_eval_app()` or `evaluate_extraction()` to
set it from the start.
